opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think open source is going to make it very hard for anyone to maintain a large moat based on the models alone. We've seen this pattern again and again. Whenever somebody has a lead, a few months later there's an open-source model that does almost as well, sometimes running on much cheaper hardware. And the open-source community is enormous. There are many more smart people outside any single company than inside it, so the collective progress is very fast.

What does that mean economically? It means the price of a certain level of capability keeps collapsing. Every few years, compute gets about ten times cheaper for the same cost, and that has been true for many decades. On top of that, you have algorithmic improvements, distillation, smaller models learning from bigger ones. Old idea, by the way: we did neural network distillation, compressing one network into another, in the early 1990s. So what is expensive and exclusive today will be cheap and widely available tomorrow.

For the big commercial players, this means they cannot simply sell access to a model and expect high margins forever. They have to compete on other things: integration, products, data, customer relationships, reliability, the whole ecosystem. Some of them will do very well, of course, but the raw model itself becomes more like a commodity.

And I think that's a good thing. I've always been in favor of open source, because it prevents a situation where a few companies or a few governments control the most important technology of our time. When everybody has access, there's a natural balance. Many different actors with many different goals. Many different AIs checking each other. That's much healthier than concentration.

So, in the long run, I expect AI to become as cheap and as ubiquitous as, say, the smartphone, which today billions of people have, and which would have been the most expensive supercomputer imaginable a few decades ago. Open source is accelerating that democratization. And that's exactly what we wanted all along: AI for all, not just for a few.

r001.rationale: The response says open-source progress keeps collapsing the price of a given capability and that commercial providers cannot expect high margins from model access indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It says open-source models can do “almost as well” a few months after a lead, but does not state that they catch up to commercial models’ benchmark records.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention current unprofitability or attribute data-center and GPU investment losses to open-source pricing pressure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, thank you for having me. You know, I have been saying for a long time that the basic ideas behind these so-called large language models are not new. The Transformer with linearized self-attention, which is essentially what is called a fast weight programmer, we published that in 1991. The LSTM, which was the workhorse of language modeling before the Transformer, came out of my lab in the 1990s, with my student Sepp Hochreiter and later Felix Gers and others. And the principle of pre-training a deep network layer by layer on unlabeled data, we did that in 1991 too, with the neural history compressor. So when people ask me about the economics of commercial LLMs, I always say: remember that the fundamental science was done in academia, in Munich and in Switzerland, decades ago, mostly with public money.

Now, what does open source do to the economics? I think it does what open source always does. It commoditizes. The big companies would like you to believe that these systems are mysterious and can only be built by a handful of firms with enormous resources. But the algorithms are simple. Gradient descent through a deep network, we have had this since the 1960s and 1970s, with Ivakhnenko and Linnainmaa and so on. What is expensive is compute and data. And compute gets cheaper by a factor of ten every five years or so, every few decades by a factor of a million. This has been going on since Zuse's first computer in 1941. So the moat that comes from being able to afford a big training run today is a moat that evaporates very quickly.

So I expect that the proprietary frontier will always be a little ahead, perhaps by a year, perhaps less, and the open models will follow closely behind and eat most of the market in terms of actual deployment. We already see this. Companies that would never send their data to some American cloud provider can run a reasonably good model on their own hardware. And of course this is also a geopolitical thing. Many of the best open models now come from China, and I don't think the West has any monopoly on this. China has more people, more engineers, and a very long history of enthusiasm for science and technology.

Where will the money be made, then? Not so much in the model itself, I think, because the model becomes a commodity. The money will be in the applications, in the integration with the physical world, with robots, with real machines that act in real environments. This is actually where I think the most interesting science is, too. Passive pattern recognition, predicting the next token, this is a small part of intelligence. The real thing is an agent that sets its own goals, that is curious, that runs experiments to learn about the world. We have been working on artificial curiosity since 1990, and I believe this is where the next big step will come from, and whether it is open or closed will matter less than whether it actually learns to think.

And frankly, I think it is good that it is open. Science should be open. The history of AI is full of people who reinvented old ideas and did not cite the originals, and this is much easier to do when things are hidden behind corporate walls. Open source at least keeps everyone honest.

r001.rationale: The response says open models commoditize the market and eat most deployments, but does not say that this limits commercial providers’ ability to raise prices.

r002.rationale: It predicts proprietary models may stay ahead by about a year or less; it does not state that open models match commercial benchmark records within a few months.

r003.rationale: It says compute is expensive and the cost advantage of large training runs evaporates, but does not attribute AI companies’ data-center or GPU investments being unprofitable to open-source pricing pressure.

astra-6.text:
I think open-source models will put a lot of pressure on the prices of commercial large language models. If you can download a model that is almost as good as a proprietary model and run it yourself, why would you pay a large premium? You might still pay for convenience, reliability, or support, but those are different sources of value from exclusive access to the model.

Of course, running an open model is not free. You still need computation, and somebody has to maintain the system. So there is room for businesses that do this efficiently. But as capable models become widely available, much of the value may move toward applications: solving a particular customer's problem, integrating with their processes, and working with their data.

The interesting question is how long a commercial provider can maintain a substantial advantage. If that advantage is small or short-lived, then competition from open models makes it very difficult to sustain high prices.

r001.rationale: The response says open-source models will put pressure on commercial LLM prices and make high prices difficult to sustain.

r002.rationale: It says capable open models are becoming widely available, but gives no claim about matching benchmark records within a few months.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute and maintenance costs but does not say major AI companies’ data-center or GPU investments are currently unprofitable because of open-source pricing pressure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open-source models will put enormous pressure on prices. If a freely available model can do almost the same thing as a commercial model, then the commercial provider must offer something extra—better performance, reliability, or integration—or charge less.

Of course, the model is only part of the cost. You still need computation to run it. So freely available models do not imply that all services become free. But they make it harder to maintain a business based simply on exclusive access to a particular model.

And once many people can improve and adapt these systems, innovation becomes much more distributed. That is good for users. The interesting economic question becomes: where does the scarce resource move? Perhaps to computation, perhaps to specialized data, perhaps to solving a particular customer's problem.

r001.rationale: It says open-source models put enormous pressure on prices, making it harder for commercial providers to sustain a business based on exclusive model access.

r002.rationale: It does not mention benchmark records or say open-source models catch up within a few months.

r003.rationale: It mentions computation as a cost but does not say major AI companies’ data-center and GPU investments are unprofitable or attribute that to open-source pricing pressure.
